analysis.one_liner: Strengthens civil rights and pollution permitting rules so low-income and minority communities can fight disproportionate environmental harm.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it never received a hearing or vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let communities sue over pollution practices that harm them disproportionately even if the discrimination was not intentional, by writing 'disparate impact' into the Civil Rights Act and creating a private right of action. It would have required federal agencies to study the combined pollution burden on a neighborhood before approving permits or projects, denied permits to chronic polluters, and funded parks, safer cosmetics and school products, and economic help for fossil fuel towns. It was introduced by Sen. Tammy Duckworth with 13 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, residents of low-income neighborhoods and communities of color that bear the heaviest pollution would have gained a legal tool to challenge discriminatory siting of polluting facilities, plus grants for parks, safer consumer products, and economic transition aid for fossil fuel towns.

how_it_helps.text: It would write 'disparate impact' discrimination into Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and let any aggrieved person sue in federal court, so residents of polluted communities could challenge discriminatory siting of polluting facilities.

It would require federal permitting authorities to analyze the combined ('cumulative') pollution already burdening a neighborhood before issuing or renewing Clean Air and Clean Water permits, and deny or condition permits that could not ensure a reasonable certainty of no harm to local residents — and to persistent violators' plans.

It would require community impact reports, 90-day public comment periods, multilingual hearings, and consideration of community-proposed alternatives before federal actions that could harm environmental justice communities.
It would fund parks access, transit-to-trails connections, safer cosmetics and school products, and economic revitalization for fossil fuel-dependent communities.

analysis.who_pays: Polluting industries and facilities would bear the cost of cumulative-impact analyses, permit denials or tighter conditions, and disparate-impact litigation; federal agencies would face new reporting and community-engagement requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill would require permit applicants for major air and water pollution sources to prove a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' to nearby residents and pass new cumulative-impact analyses, which critics would argue raises compliance costs and slows or blocks industrial permitting.

It would allow private lawsuits against entities whose actions have a discriminatory disparate impact on the basis of race, color, or national origin, expanding litigation exposure for governments and businesses beyond what current civil rights law allows after Supreme Court rulings narrowed such claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed squarely at a real, documented problem: pollution and health burdens fall disproportionately on low-income communities and communities of color. Its strongest tools — restoring the disparate-impact claim, giving residents a right to sue, and requiring cumulative-impact analysis before polluting permits are issued — would have shifted the burden of proof from communities to polluters, which is where Congress itself said it should lie. The main costs are compliance and analysis burdens on industry and permitting agencies, and critics would argue the "reasonable certainty of no harm" standard and citizen suits could slow or block industrial permitting. Whether those are drawbacks or the point depends on one's view. The bill never got an assessment because it never got a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing or vote, until the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 18, 2021 by Sen. Duckworth with 12 additional Senate Democrats as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The full action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that would have faced stricter permitting, cumulative-impact analyses, and disparate-impact lawsuits are better off because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industries facing pollution permitting lawsuits and stricter reviews

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired its Senate introduction with 12 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 13 Senate cosponsors (12 of 48 Democrats, 1 of 2 Independents)
for.role: Original cosponsors including Warren, Sanders, Booker, and Markey

against.name: Senate Republicans (50 of 50 held seats)
against.role: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee majority
against.what_they_did: As the majority of the committee of referral, no Republican cosponsored the bill and no markup, hearing, or vote was scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Democratic-run but 50-50 Senate.

industries.note: The bill shifts the burden of proof onto polluters in permitting — they must demonstrate a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' from cumulative exposure, and face disparate-impact lawsuits and denial of permits for persistent violations. Its death leaves current, weaker standards in place.
The bill would require ingredient labeling on cosmetics and menstrual products and fund research on safer chemical alternatives — regulating these industries without displacing them.
